name: Fatima Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, AI firms, unions, parties and government. What you say here is confidential. How does a normal day go?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start with a folder of transport-company invoices and a mug of tea before anyone asks where the fuel receipts went. I'm 43 and a junior accountant at Oak Bridge Tax; I have a bachelor's degree in accounting, but I still ask the senior to check my tax adjustments. I enjoy catching a duplicate fuel bill, and I dislike the call where I must tell a driver-owner a return is late because I missed a page.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what is home like, including money and the tools you use?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Tariq does carpentry jobs, and our children are eight and eleven; their shoes seem to wear out at the same time. We have a mortgage, about five months of bills saved, my accounting pay is typical for the job, and there are some other firms nearby. I use AI every day to group fuel invoices and draft client questions, then check the originals. I like trying a new tool early, but our family budget comes before a gadget or a course with no paid job behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the drivers that a tidy invoice list helps us finish their returns sooner. I'd still check a fuel receipt against the bank record before I ask anyone to pay tax on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think Oak Bridge keeps me, but I'm junior and still make mistakes, and Tariq's carpentry work has quiet weeks. Five months saved helps, yet a quiet month for both of us would still hurt the mortgage account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep sorting invoices with my daily AI tool and checking each doubtful entry against the original. In the first year I'd move sixty a month from our weekend takeaway budget into savings while Tariq's jobs are steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the household's uneven pay, even if AI stays modest. The mortgage does not have a quiet week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which entry do you check twice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fuel card purchase can appear in the driver's list and again in the bank export. I open the receipt before removing either line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why only sixty a month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some weeks Tariq has two carpentry jobs and some weeks none. I won't promise a hundred we might need for school meals.

I would show drivers a **clean return** without hiding odd entries.
think: My **junior job** seems likely to stay, but I still make errors.
Tariq’s **uneven carpentry pay** makes our mortgage budget tight.
do: Keep checking **fuel receipts** against the bank export after AI sorting.
Save **sixty monthly** from takeaways while carpentry income stays steady.
feel: She feels **uneasy** about uneven household pay and a mortgage.
S0.quote: The mortgage does not have a quiet week.
fieldNote: Her concern in the plateau is **irregular carpentry income** as much as her own junior standing.
She uses AI **daily already** and checks duplicate fuel card entries against original receipts.

steps.text: Keep checking fuel receipts after daily AI invoice sorting
Save sixty monthly from takeaways while carpentry income stays steady

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the partners we need to see the software on the untidy driver files, not just a perfect demonstration. I would volunteer to test it if the firm pays the hours and lets the senior review mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It can do the invoice grouping, checking and letters that fill my day. I am quick with tools, but I'm still a junior, so I expect fewer hours if the partners decide one reviewer can cover two desks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a paid three-week trial on closed transport returns, logging every duplicate fuel bill the system misses. In the first year of strong change, if my paid days fall below four, I'd apply for posted accounts assistant jobs at the nearby depot companies and keep whatever funded hours Oak Bridge offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because a day less pay would touch the mortgage. I can learn the system, but I cannot learn away a missing day on the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the trial is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the approved invoice sorter and my paper check, and ask for another paid chance later. I wouldn't upload client records into an unapproved tool from home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tariq do if your hours fell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He could take a Saturday carpentry job only if a client books it and I cover the children. We would not count a possible job in the mortgage budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that full AGI in 2028 can prepare returns and check invoices for less, so the partners owe us an honest staffing answer. We should tell clients who will still sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The desk work is exposed in 2028, before robots reach hands-on carpentry around 2031. I expect my junior hours to shrink sharply, and Tariq's carpentry wage could be less steady when robots spread later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add two hundred a month to our emergency fund now by postponing the kitchen renovation. In the first year after 2028, if Oak Bridge ends my post, I'd apply for advertised salaried depot finance roles and take confirmed paid weekend bookkeeping only when Tariq can cover the children; I'd keep the five-month reserve for mortgage payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because my wage could fall and Tariq's work might later change too. Five months is a cushion, not a replacement for both jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a new qualification?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a posted paid depot role requires it and an employer funds the study time. I won't spend the mortgage buffer to collect a certificate without a start date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if weekend bookkeeping isn't booked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay home with the children and keep searching salaried posts. I would not call a neighbour's maybe a client in our budget.

I would tell clients who **signs returns** after AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years allows a proper test of which transport clients pay for help with cash flow, not just annual tax forms. I would want a named salary behind any new role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when AGI reaches the desk in 2031, with children still needing us and a mortgage to pay. Even the cash-flow advice might be cheap then, but a few years gives me room to see what clients actually renew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Oak Bridge for a paid pilot of monthly fuel-cost reviews with four transport clients next year, with the firm keeping the fees and the senior checking my first reports. In the first year after 2031, I'd stay on that salaried service only if three clients renew at fees covering staff time; otherwise I'd apply for posted salaried depot finance jobs while keeping any funded firm hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but I can test a paid offer before relying on it. I do not want to move my children for a job that is only a rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show a transport client?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare fuel bought with routes driven, then ask why a vehicle costs more per mile than the others. If the owner won't pay for a second month, I would write that down rather than call the visit a success.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for the depot role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a written salary offer names the start date and leaves one of us home for school pickup. There are some depots nearby, so I'd try those before moving houses.

I would require **three renewals** covering staff time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us time to find paid work that a transport owner will still want a person to explain. It also gives our children time to see us handle change without selling the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036 I might still owe on the mortgage, though ten years could build a bigger reserve. AGI reaches my thinking desk then; robots around 2039 might later change Tariq's carpentry jobs, so neither income is guaranteed forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put an extra hundred a month against mortgage principal while both incomes are steady and ask the firm for paid time to learn transport payroll disputes. In the first year after 2036, if Oak Bridge no longer funds my role, I'd apply for posted salaried payroll jobs and accept only a written offer with a start date and a wage covering the mortgage; meanwhile I'd keep any paid firm hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy, but ten years of paid work could make the loan smaller. I can try a new specialty while a wage still arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn on paid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd match drivers' shifts to wage slips with the senior present, and find which overtime payment was missed. I would not buy a private course before a paid employer place exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try to retire early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the children's schooling and the mortgage still need a wage. I would rather work well at 53 than borrow from our five-month reserve to stop early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because junior hours could go before we have made the mortgage smaller. An honest staffing answer, a posted paid depot job and a way to keep the children cared for would help. I can test a tool before breakfast, but I cannot test a missing wage on my family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether firms will pay juniors to learn on real files when software handles the easy ones. Skill comes from corrected mistakes, not from a button that hides them.

headlineQuote: I can test a tool before breakfast, but I cannot test a missing wage on my family.
portrait: Fatima, **43**, is a junior transport-accounts worker at Oak Bridge Tax with an accounting bachelor’s degree.
She earns **typical pay**, has five months saved, two school-age children, a mortgage and some nearby firms.
She uses AI **daily** on fuel invoices, then checks receipts while Tariq’s carpentry income varies.
She fears **2028 junior-hour loss** and tests paid firm services with renewal and childcare conditions.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut her junior hours before the family reduces its mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: An **honest staffing answer**, a posted paid depot job and reliable childcare would help.
